content:
**Quick answer:** Morning stiffness with arthritis can happen because joints have been relatively still overnight, while inflammation can also contribute in inflammatory types of arthritis. Gentle movement, warmth, pacing your morning and gradually increasing activity may help. Persistent, prolonged or worsening stiffness should be discussed with a healthcare professional.

## Why joints are stiff after waking

One reason is simple: you have spent several hours relatively still, and when you start moving again, your joints and the muscles around them initially feel less flexible. Inflammation can also play an important role, particularly in inflammatory arthritis, so morning stiffness usually has several contributing factors rather than one simple cause.

Morning stiffness can occur with osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis and other conditions, and other musculoskeletal problems can cause it too. Stiffness alone does not confirm a diagnosis. If it is new, persistent or accompanied by swollen joints or other symptoms, seek medical advice rather than diagnosing yourself.

## Why the length of stiffness matters

Healthcare professionals often ask how long your stiffness lasts because the pattern helps them understand your symptoms. NHS information describes morning stiffness associated with osteoarthritis as generally lasting less than about 30 minutes, while rheumatoid arthritis, an autoimmune inflammatory condition, often causes stiffness that lasts longer after waking or inactivity, sometimes with swelling, warmth, tenderness, fatigue, several affected joints, or joints on both sides of the body.

Duration alone cannot diagnose either condition. But if you are seeing your GP about joint symptoms, keeping a short record of how long morning stiffness lasts, which joints are affected, whether joints are swollen, whether movement helps, and whether the pattern is changing can help you describe things clearly. Persistent joint swelling with prolonged morning stiffness is a reason to speak to your GP.

## Start moving before you get up

You do not have to wait until you are standing to start moving. If comfortable, try a few small movements while still in bed: gently open and close your hands, slowly bend and straighten your fingers, move your ankles up and down, gently bend and straighten your knees, and change position slowly. You are introducing movement, not performing a workout.

Then take the transition in stages: move your legs gently, roll towards the side of the bed, bring your legs towards the edge, use your arms for support if appropriate, sit for a moment, place your feet securely, and stand when you feel ready. If getting out of bed is regularly difficult, an occupational therapist or physiotherapist can help.

Hands can be particularly troublesome first thing: making a fist, gripping a toothbrush, fastening buttons, opening containers. Avoid immediately forcing your fingers into a tight fist if they feel very stiff; gentle opening and closing movements are usually more comfortable. If your hands are persistently swollen, hot or increasingly difficult to use, speak to a healthcare professional.

## Warmth, showers and stretching

A safely wrapped warm pack or a comfortably warm shower can feel soothing on a stiff area, and a shower can combine warmth with gentle movement as you wash and dress. Protect your skin, avoid excessive heat, and take extra care with reduced sensation, circulation problems or reduced balance; grab rails or a shower seat may be useful for some people after an appropriate assessment. Heat provides comfort, but it does not treat the underlying cause of arthritis.

Cold and heat suit different people and symptoms. Warmth is often chosen when stiffness is the main problem; cold may feel more soothing when a joint is particularly painful or swollen.

Gentle stretching may feel helpful, but a stiff joint does not need to be pushed aggressively to "loosen it up". Move slowly, stay within a comfortable range, avoid bouncing, and stop for sharp or unusual pain.

## Pace the morning, prepare the night before

Trying to complete everything quickly makes an already difficult morning more demanding. Allow extra time, move gently, complete tasks in stages, and sit or pause when useful.

Preparing the night before reduces the decisions and physical tasks waiting for you: lay out clothes, prepare breakfast items, pack a work bag, organise medication according to your prescribed routine, place frequently used items within easy reach, prepare anything needed for children or caring responsibilities, and check transport arrangements.

For dressing, consider sitting down, easy-to-manage fastenings, a long-handled shoehorn and keeping clothing within reach. For breakfast, lightweight cups and pans, easy-grip utensils and accessible storage all reduce unnecessary strain on stiff hands and joints. The aim is not to avoid using your joints, but to reduce unnecessary strain.

## Should you exercise first thing?

It depends on how you feel. Some people prefer gentle mobility movements shortly after waking and leave more demanding strengthening or aerobic exercise until later. There is no prize for completing your hardest exercise session immediately after waking.

Regular appropriate activity during the day helps maintain joint movement, muscle strength, mobility and general health, and long periods of complete inactivity can contribute to stiffness. For osteoarthritis, NICE recommends therapeutic exercise tailored to the individual.

## Driving, stress, sleep and medication

Do not drive until you can safely control the vehicle. Morning stiffness may affect your ability to turn your head, grip the steering wheel, operate pedals or react quickly, so give yourself enough time to move comfortably first. If arthritis significantly affects your ability to drive safely, seek appropriate medical and driving advice.

Pain, stiffness, fatigue and poor sleep interact: poor sleep leaves you with less energy for dealing with pain, and arthritis symptoms themselves can disturb sleep. If poor sleep is becoming a regular problem, discuss it with your GP.

And do not start, stop, increase, reduce or change the timing of prescribed medication because of morning stiffness without appropriate medical advice. If stiffness is becoming more severe or lasting much longer than usual, tell your GP, pharmacist or rheumatology team, because the pattern may help them assess whether your treatment needs reviewing.

## When stiffness should be checked

Speak to a GP if stiffness is new and persistent, lasting longer than usual, affecting several joints, accompanied by swelling or unexplained fatigue, affecting both sides of your body, interfering substantially with everyday life, or a significant change in your usual symptoms. Early assessment can be particularly important when inflammatory arthritis is suspected. Increased stiffness can also form part of a flare, particularly if pain, swelling or fatigue are more noticeable too.

> **When it is urgent**
>
> Seek urgent medical advice for a joint that becomes suddenly very painful, hot or significantly swollen, particularly with fever, shivering or feeling generally unwell; that can sometimes indicate infection or another urgent condition, not normal morning stiffness. The same applies to sudden inability to bear weight, severe swelling, sudden weakness, significant new numbness, or loss of bladder or bowel control.

## Key takeaways

- Morning stiffness is common and may follow hours of relative inactivity; inflammation can contribute, particularly in inflammatory arthritis.
- The duration of stiffness is useful information for your GP but cannot diagnose arthritis by itself.
- Gentle movement before and after getting out of bed, warmth and a slower, staged start may help.
- Preparing clothes, breakfast items and essentials the night before reduces morning strain.
- Do not force stiff joints, do not change prescribed medication yourself, and get persistent, prolonged or changing stiffness assessed.

## Frequently asked questions

### Why is arthritis worse in the morning?

Several hours of relative inactivity overnight can contribute to stiffness when you first move. Inflammation may also contribute, particularly in inflammatory arthritis, and different types of arthritis produce different patterns.

### How long does morning stiffness last with osteoarthritis?

NHS guidance notes that morning stiffness associated with osteoarthritis generally lasts less than about 30 minutes. Symptoms vary, and stiffness duration alone cannot diagnose the condition.

### Can morning stiffness mean rheumatoid arthritis?

Prolonged morning stiffness can occur with rheumatoid arthritis, particularly alongside joint swelling, pain and other symptoms. It does not confirm rheumatoid arthritis by itself, so seek medical assessment if you are concerned.

### Should I exercise as soon as I wake up?

You can begin with gentle mobility movements if comfortable, but you do not have to complete a full exercise session immediately. Some people prefer to wait until their joints feel less stiff.

## A gentle next step

A gentler start, comfortable movement, warmth, pacing and practical preparation can make mornings more manageable. Pay attention to changes in your symptoms rather than assuming every episode of stiffness is simply part of arthritis; your GP, physiotherapist, rheumatology team or occupational therapist can provide individual support. You can also explore practical arthritis information and support from Living With Arthritis.
